Simulating superconductivity in mixed-dimensional t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} bilayers
with neural quantum states

Hannah Lange Email: hannah.lange@lmu.de Affiliation: Department of Physics and Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics (ASC), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, München D-80333, Germany Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institute for Quantum Optics, Hans-Kopfermann-Str.1, Garching D-85748, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, München D-80799, Germany    Ao Chen Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA    Antoine Georges Affiliation: Collège de France, Université PSL, 11 place Marcelin Berthelot, 75005 Paris, France Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA Affiliation: Centre de Physique Théorique, Ecole Polytechnique, CNRS, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91128 Palaiseau Cedex, France Affiliation: DQMP, Université de Genève, 24 quai Ernest Ansermet, CH-1211 Genève, Suisse    Fabian Grusdt Affiliation: Department of Physics and Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics (ASC), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, München D-80333, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, München D-80799, Germany    Annabelle Bohrdt Affiliation: Department of Physics and Arnold Sommerfeld Center for Theoretical Physics (ASC), Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Theresienstr. 37, München D-80333, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, München D-80799, Germany    Christopher Roth Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York 10010, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Motivated by the recent discovery of superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7 (LNO) under pressure, we study a mixed-dimensional (mixD) bilayer t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} model, which has been proposed as an effective low-energy description of LNO. Using neural quantum states (NQS), and in particular Gutzwiller-projected Hidden Fermion Pfaffian State, we access the ground-state properties on large lattices up to 8×8×28\times 8\times 2 sites. We show that this model exhibits superconductivity across a wide range of dopings and couplings, and analyze the pairing behavior in detail. We identify a crossover from tightly bound, Bose-Einstein-condensed interlayer pairs at strong interlayer exchange to more spatially extended Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer-like pairs as the interlayer exchange is decreased. Furthermore, upon tuning the intralayer exchange, we observe a sharp transition from interlayer ss-wave pairing to intralayer dd-wave pairing, consistent with a first-order change in the pairing symmetry. We verify that our simulations are accurate by comparing with matrix product state simulations on coupled ladders. Our results represent the first simulation of a fermionic multi-orbital system with NQS, and provide the first evidence for superconductivity in two-dimensonal bilayers using high-precision numerics. These findings provide insight into superconductivity in bilayer nickelates and cold atom quantum simulation platforms.

Since the discovery of high-TcT_{c} superconductivity [2] nearly four decades ago, extensive research efforts have revealed a rich variety of unconventional superconductors. In 2023, a superconducting transition at Tc=80​KT_{c}=80\,\mathrm{K} was reported in the bilayer Ruddlesen-Popper bilayer perovskite nickelate compound La3Ni2O7 (LNO) under applied pressure [43, 48]. Subsequent studies have shown that the physics of LNO, with dz2d_{z^{2}} and dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} orbitals contributing at the Fermi level, is governed by strong electronic correlations [25, 13, 6] and can be effectively captured by a mixed-dimensional (mixD) t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} bilayer model with magnetic inter- and intralayer exchange J⟂J_{\perp} and J∥J_{\parallel} but hopping restricted to intralayer contributions t∥t_{\parallel} [35, 34, 27], see Fig. 1a. Beyond their relevance to LNO, mixD models also capture physics relevant to Kondo models and cuprate superconductors [23].

Motivated by these developments, unbiased numerical simulations of mixed-dimensional bilayers constitute an important step toward understanding the pairing mechanism in these systems and, more broadly, the development of a theoretical description of unconventional superconductivity. In the regime of dominant interlayer coupling J⟂J_{\perp} and low hole-doping, pairing in mixD bilayers is well understood and arises from the interplay of the kinetic energy of doped holes and the magnetic background consisting of singlets formed on the rungs of the bilayer: In contrast to isolated holes, pairs of holes can move through the system without disrupting this singlet background, leading to the formation of tightly-bound hole pairs with large binding energies on the order of J⟂J_{\perp} [3]. As a result, pair formation can be observed up to relatively high temperatures, as demonstrated in cold-atom realizations of mixD systems [17, 14]. Away from this limit, mixD bilayers have been anticipated to host a rich phase diagram, including a crossover from a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) regime to Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of tightly bound pairs, as discussed for single or coupled ladders in Refs. [4, 19, 20, 41], as well as multiple pairing symmetries [28, 12, 34, 45, 5, 46]. Given the strong pairing energy scales, this rich phase diagram may be readily observable in cold atom simulations.

Nevertheless, accurate numerical studies of mixD systems remain highly challenging. Apart from mean-field and dynamical mean-field theory approaches [12, 33], investigations of the mixD model have largely relied on matrix product state (MPS) methods, which are typically restricted to ladder geometries [42, 35, 20] or coupled ladders [41, 19, 46] and open boundary conditions. To the best of our knowledge, a fully two-dimensional numerical study of the mixD t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} model that captures strong correlation effects beyond mean-field-type treatments is still lacking.

Here, we address this challenge by employing a relatively new class of variational wave functions known as neural quantum states (NQS) [22, 30], and adapting them to mixD t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} bilayer systems. Specifically, we combine the Hidden Fermion Pfaffian State ansatz [10] – which can naturally encode charge pairing if required, e.g. in the strong-J⟂J_{\perp} regime – with the concept of Gutzwiller projection [16, 21]. We demonstrate that this approach enables us to investigate the rich pairing physics of the mixD model on fully two-dimensional bilayers while explicitly accounting for strong local correlations.

The mixD t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} model we study is given by

+J∥∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩,μ(𝐒^𝐢,μ⋅𝐒^𝐣,μ−14n^𝐢,μn^𝐣,μ)\displaystyle+J_{\parallel}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i,j}\rangle,\mu}\left(\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{\mathbf{j},\mu}-\frac{1}{4}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{j},\mu}\right)
+J⟂∑𝐢(𝐒^𝐢,0⋅𝐒^𝐢,1−14n^𝐢,0n^𝐢,1),\displaystyle+J_{\perp}\sum_{\mathbf{i}}\left(\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{\mathbf{i},0}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{\mathbf{i},1}-\frac{1}{4}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i},0}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i},1}\right),

with c^𝐢,μ,σ(†)\hat{c}^{(\dagger)}_{\mathbf{i},\mu,\sigma} the annihilation (creation) operators for fermions in layer μ=0,1\mu=0,1 and with spin σ=±1/2\sigma=\pm 1/2, and 𝐒^𝐢,μ\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{\mathbf{i},\mu} (n^𝐢,μ\hat{n}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}) the respective spin (density) operators. DFT calculations suggest t∥≈0.5​eVt_{\parallel}\approx 0.5\,\mathrm{eV}, J∥≈0.2​eVJ_{\parallel}\approx 0.2\,\mathrm{eV} and J⟂≈0.3​eVJ_{\perp}\approx 0.3\,\mathrm{eV} for LNO [35].

Our Gutzwiller-projected Hidden Fermion Pfaffian States (G-HFPS) allow to simulate ground states of fully two-dimensional (2D) mixD bilayers on lattices as large as 8×8×28\times 8\times 2 and with periodic boundary conditions (PBC). We study the regime of J⟂/t∥=0.6J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=0.6, J∥/t∥=0.4J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.4 and δ=0.5\delta=0.5 doping relevant to LNO, as well as perform scans through the phase diagram of the mixD bilayer model at different dopings, observing the theoretically anticipated BEC-to-BCS crossover [4, 20, 45] as a function of t∥/J⟂t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp} and a change of pairing symmetry from interlayer ss-wave (s⟂s_{\perp}) to intralayer dd-wave (d∥d_{\parallel}) as a function of J∥/t∥J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}. To our knowledge, this is the first study of the mixD tt-JJ bilayer model in 2D that captures strong correlation effects beyond mean-field ansätze. Furthermore, while accurate results for fermionic single-layer systems have been achieved using determinant and Pfaffian based NQS recently [21, 15, 26, 10, 38], for the first time a bilayer system is simulated using NQS. We observe that, due to the strong pairing inherent to this system, the underlying pairing wave function in form of the Pfaffian becomes particularly advantageous over a determinant construction.

Method.— We apply a variational wave function that is conceptually similar to a mean-field pairing wave function, as used for the mixD bilayer in Ref. [12], but incorporate correlation effects by making use of neural networks [10, 32, 38] in combination with Gutzwiller projection [16, 21]. To include correlations using neural networks, we expand the physical Hilbert space consisting of NN orbitals and NvN_{v} visible fermions by additional NhN_{h} hidden fermions, Ntot=Nv+NhN_{\mathrm{tot}}=N_{v}+N_{h}. The pairing wave function in this expanded Hilbert space – the Hidden Fermion Pfaffian State (HFPS) [10] – becomes

ψ⁡(𝐧)=J𝜽​(𝐧)⋅pf​(𝐅v​v𝐅𝜽v​h​(𝐧)−𝐅𝜽v​h​(𝐧)T𝐅h​h),\psi({\bf n})=J_{\bm{\theta}}({\bf n})\cdot\mathrm{pf}\begin{pmatrix}{\bf F}^{vv}&{\bf F}_{\bm{\theta}}^{vh}({\bf n})\\ -{\bf F}^{vh}_{\bm{\theta}}({\bf n})^{T}&{\bf F}^{hh}\end{pmatrix}, (2)

for a Fock space configuration of physical fermions, 𝐧\mathbf{n}, and pf\mathrm{pf} denoting the computation of a Pfaffian. The matrices 𝐅v​v{\bf F}^{vv}, 𝐅𝜽v​h​(𝐧){\bf F}_{\bm{\theta}}^{vh}({\bf n}) and 𝐅h​h{\bf F}^{hh} represent the respective couplings between visible and hidden fermions, where the configuration dependent hidden contributions are represented by a neural network with parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}, either by representing 𝐅𝜽v​h​(𝐧){\bf F}_{\bm{\theta}}^{vh}({\bf n}) directly or by absorbing the configuration dependence of the hidden orbitals 𝐅h​h\mathbf{F}^{hh} into the Jastrow factor J𝜽​(𝐧)J_{\bm{\theta}}({\mathbf{n}}) without loss of generality, which tends to improve training stability [10]. Note that ψ\psi can also express a hidden fermion determinant state (HFDS) [37] as derived in Ref. [10].

For the configuration dependent orbitals, we use a Group Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN), allowing us to incorporate translation, rotation, reflection and spin-parity symmetries within a single neural network forward pass [44, 39], and construct a corresponding symmetric state ψsym\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}, see SM [44]. The final wave function constructed here is given after Gutzwiller projection ψG−HFPS​(𝐧)=𝒫^G​ψsym​(𝐧)\psi_{\mathrm{G-HFPS}}(\mathbf{n})=\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{G}\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbf{n}), similar to the Gutzwiller-projected HFDS that were proposed in Ref. [21].

Without hidden variables, Eq. (2) is the mean-field solution of BCS-like Hamiltonians including pairing terms of the form ΔΓMF​c^𝐢†​c^𝐣†+h.c.\Delta^{\mathrm{MF}}_{\Gamma}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{j}}+\mathrm{h.c.} (the Pfaffian is reduced to a determinant for ΔΓMF=0\Delta^{\mathrm{MF}}_{\Gamma}=0 [1]). For all regimes of the phase diagram and a suitable choice of pairing symmetry Γ\Gamma, we find that initialization of the HFPS such that the visible part is the solution to a Hamiltonian with a pairing field, ΔΓMF>0\Delta^{\mathrm{MF}}_{\Gamma}>0, yields the best energies after the full training of the HFPS, see SM [44].

Ground State Energies.— The ground state energies obtained with the G-HFPS with Nh=4N_{h}=4 and a GCNN feature dimension f=10f=10 (corresponding to #​P≈300,000\#P\approx 300,000 trainable parameters) are shown in Fig. 1b for quarter-filling (δ=Nv/N=0.5\delta=N_{v}/N=0.5) and two exemplary points in the phase diagram. On the left, we compare the energies to results from MPS with total spin and charge conservation in each layer and bond dimension up to χ=4096\chi=4096 on coupled ladders up to size N=32×2×2N=32\times 2\times 2. Note that for the MPS, we are restricted to OBC in the long direction, while for the NQS we focus on PBC due to the translational symmetry inherent to the GCNN. This discrepancy leads to visibly lower energies for the smaller system but is negligibly small for the longer system: From the increase of the MPS energy from Lx=8→32L_{x}=8\to 32, we can estimate the energy for each of the four missing bonds in xx-direction as c=|E⁡(Lx=32)−E⁡(Lx=8)|/(4​Δ​Lx)≈0.02​t∥c=|E(L_{x}=32)-E(L_{x}=8)|/(4\Delta L_{x})\approx 0.02\,t_{\parallel}, and hence the estimated energy difference in Fig 1b resulting from the different boundary choices is on the order of 4​c/N=0.0007​t∥4c/N=0.0007\,t_{\parallel} for the long system. Overall, the agreement with the MPS energy for these larger systems with Lx=32L_{x}=32 is very good: For the system with J⟂/t∥=3.0J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=3.0 and J∥/t∥=0.0J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.0, a regime with tightly bound pairs on the rungs of the bilayer – a relatively local state, which is favorable for the MPS representation – the MPS energies are slightly lower with an energy difference of Δ​E/N=0.004​t∥\Delta E/N=0.004\,t_{\parallel}. For the regime more relevant to LNO with J⟂/t∥=0.6J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=0.6 and J∥/t∥=0.4J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.4, lower energies than the MPS energies are obtained with Δ​E/N=−0.0002​t∥\Delta E/N=-0.0002\,t_{\parallel} on the order of 4​c/N4c/N. A more detailed analysis is given in the SM [44]. The right side of 1b shows that for the fully 2D systems, which are not accessible with MPS but with the G-HFPS, the energy per site E/NE/N remains approximately constant when increasing the system size. All errorbars denote errors of the mean and are typically smaller than the markers.

Estimation of pairing amplitudes.– In the following, we will investigate different pairing regimes such as a BEC-to-BCS crossover and a transition from interlayer ss-wave (s⟂s_{\perp}) to intralayer dd-wave (d∥d_{\parallel}) pairing. Specifically, we consider symmetrized pair creation operators

Δ^𝐢s⟂​(𝐫)\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{i}}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{r}) =12​(c^𝐢,↓​c^𝐢+(rx,ry,1),↑−c^𝐢,↑​c^𝐢+(rx,ry,1),↓),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i},\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}+(r_{x},r_{y},1),\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i},\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}+(r_{x},r_{y},1),\downarrow}\right)\,, (3)
Δ^𝐢,μd∥​(𝐫)\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}^{d_{\parallel}}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}(\mathbf{r}) =η𝐫2​(c^𝐢,↓​c^𝐢+(rx,ry,0),↑−c^𝐢,↑​c^𝐢+(rx,ry,0),↓),\displaystyle=\frac{\eta_{\mathbf{r}}}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i},\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}+(r_{x},r_{y},0),\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i},\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i}+(r_{x},r_{y},0),\downarrow}\right)\,,

with η𝐫∼x^=−η𝐫∼y^=1\ \eta_{{\mathbf{r}}\sim\hat{x}}=-\eta_{{\mathbf{r}}\sim\hat{y}}=1 and the layer-index μ\mu absorbed into the vectors 𝐢,𝐫\mathbf{i},\mathbf{r} if not stated differently. Nearest-neighbor pairs with 𝐫=(0,0,1)\mathbf{r}=(0,0,1) for Γ=s⟂\Gamma=s_{\perp} and 𝐫=(±1,0,0),(0,±1,0)\mathbf{r}=(\pm 1,0,0),\,(0,\pm 1,0) for Γ=d∥\Gamma=d_{\parallel} will be denoted by Δ^𝐢Γ:=Δ^𝐢Γ​(𝐫)||𝐫|=1\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{i}}:=\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{i}}(\mathbf{r})|_{|\mathbf{r}|=1}.

Superconductivity with symmetry Γ=s⟂,d∥\Gamma=s_{\perp},d_{\parallel} is characterized by particle-number symmetry breaking with order parameter ΔΓ​(𝐫)=1N​∑𝐢⟨Δ^𝐢Γ​(𝐫)+(Δ^𝐢Γ​(𝐫))†⟩/2≠0\Delta^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{i}}\langle\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{r})+(\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{r}))^{\dagger}\rangle/2\neq 0 or its Fourier transform ΔΓ​(𝐤)=∑𝐫ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​Δ​(𝐫)≠0\Delta^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\Delta(\mathbf{r})\neq 0. However, in finite size systems with conserved particle number, this quantity will evaluate to zero, motivating us to study the momentum space pair correlator

MΓ​(𝐤,𝐤′):=⟨⟨(Δ^Γ​(𝐤))†​Δ^Γ​(𝐤′)⟩⟩,\displaystyle M^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k^{\prime}}):=\langle\!\langle(\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k}))^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k^{\prime}})\rangle\!\rangle\,, (4)

where ⟨⟨…⟩⟩\langle\!\langle\dots\rangle\!\rangle denotes an expectation value in which contributions from unpaired particles (of the form ⟨c^†​c^⟩​⟨c^†​c^⟩\langle\hat{c}^{\dagger}\hat{c}\rangle\langle\hat{c}^{\dagger}\hat{c}\rangle) have been subtracted. Calculating the full MΓM^{\Gamma}-matrix scales with 𝒪⁡(N4)\mathcal{O}(N^{4}) and becomes too expensive for large system sizes. We overcome this problem by noting that for a superconductor, pair creation and annihilation processes should become fully decoupled in the thermodynamic limit and MΓ​(𝐤,𝐤′)M^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}) should approach rank-1 for large system sizes. In this case (as discussed in detail in Ref. [38] and SM [44]), the dominant eigenvector of MΓ​(𝐤,𝐤′)M^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}) corresponds to the order parameter ΔΓ​(𝐤)\Delta^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k}), that probes the linear response of the system to an applied pairing field, and can be accessed via a mixed real-momentum space correlator ⟨P^Γ​(𝐤)⟩\langle\hat{P}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k})\rangle given by

⟨P^Γ​(𝐤)⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{P}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k})\rangle =1⟨⟨(Δ¯Γ)†​Δ¯Γ⟩⟩1/2​⟨⟨p^Γ​(𝐤)⟩⟩,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\!\langle(\bar{\Delta}^{\Gamma})^{\dagger}\bar{\Delta}^{\Gamma}\rangle\!\rangle^{1/2}}\langle\!\langle\hat{p}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k})\rangle\!\rangle,
p^Γ​(𝐤)\displaystyle\hat{p}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k}) :=c^𝐤,1,↑†​c^−𝐤,0,↓†​Δ¯^Γ,\displaystyle:=\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{{\bf k},1,\uparrow}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{{\bf-k},0,\downarrow}{\hat{\bar{\Delta}}}^{\Gamma}, (5)
Δ¯^Γ\displaystyle\hat{\bar{\Delta}}^{\Gamma} :=1N​∑𝐥Δ^𝐥Γ≈Δ^(Lx/2,Ly/2)Γ,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{l}}\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{l}}^{\Gamma}\approx\hat{\Delta}_{(L_{x}/2,L_{y}/2)}^{\Gamma},

where the last approximation renders the calculation of ⟨P^Γ​(𝐤)⟩\langle\hat{P}^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k})\rangle tractable. We denote the corresponding Fourier transform by ⟨PΓ​(𝐫)⟩\langle P^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{r})\rangle. Another quantity that is often calculated to probe superconductivity in finite, particle number conserved systems are pairing correlations for real-space nearest neighbor pairs, |𝐫|=1|{\bf r}|=1, by considering the long-range behavior of ⟨(Δ^𝐢Γ)†​Δ^𝐣Γ⟩\langle(\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{i}})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{j}}\rangle. In contrast to these |𝐫|=1|{\bf r}|=1 pairing correlations, ⟨PΓ​(𝐫)⟩\langle P^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{r})\rangle allows us to measure how tightly-bound the Cooper pairs are while, in contrast to the full computation of MΓ​(𝐤,𝐤′)M^{\Gamma}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime}), being computationally accessible.

To decrease the computational cost and not constrain the wave function, we use reflection, spin parity and translation symmetries from now on. To keep the number of parameters comparable to before, we set Nh=8N_{h}=8 and f=18f=18. The resulting relative energy error w.r.t. the fully symmetrized system is on the order of 0.1%0.1\%, see SM [44]. Furthermore, we employ the adiabatic transport parameter update derived in Ref. [31, 44] for scans of the phase diagram at fixed δ\delta.

BEC-to-BCS crossover.— We first study the crossover from tightly bound pairs forming a BEC at t∥<J⟂t_{\parallel}<J_{\perp} to more spatially extended BCS-like Cooper pairs at large t∥>J⟂t_{\parallel}>J_{\perp}. More formally, we characterize the crossover by defining the average interparticle distance at doping δ\delta,

lδ=(1−δ)−1/2.\displaystyle l_{\delta}=(1-\delta)^{-1/2}. (6)

The system is considered to be in the BEC regime as long as lδl_{\delta} is larger than the size of the pairs extracted from Eq. (5) [4].

The resulting phase diagram is sketched as a function of t∥/J⟂t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp} and hole doping δ\delta in Fig. 2a. In the extreme cases of very low and very high δ\delta, the crossover is shifted to large t∥/J⟂t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}, which can be understood as follows: For high doping, we note that lδl_{\delta} grows with the hole doping δ\delta, up to lδ→1=∞l_{\delta\to 1}=\infty, pushing the crossover to t∥/J⟂→∞t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}\to\infty. At low doping δ≈0\delta\approx 0, the effective intralayer hopping t∥efft_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{eff}} is suppressed as the double occupancy constraint becomes more restrictive, again increasing the value of t∥/J⟂t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp} at which the crossover takes place.

A BEC-to-BCS crossover in the mixD setting was already anticipated in [41, 4], suggested by mean-field and coupled ladder calculations, and a similar crossover was moreover studied by introducing a repulsive term on the rungs for ladder systems using MPS [20, 19, 45] and for 2D systems on the mean-field level [5]. However, a fully two-dimensional study including correlation effects beyond MF-like ansätze has been outstanding.

In the following, we use the G-HFPS to study the phase diagram sketched in Fig. 2a. We fix J∥/t∥=0.4J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.4 and first consider δ=0.5\delta=0.5 relevant to LNO. For strong J⟂J_{\perp}, tightly bound pairs of charges form with binding energies on the order of J⟂J_{\perp}. Hence, t∥/J⟂→0t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}\to 0 gives rise to interlayer pairs that behave as bosonic bound states with momentum zero and hence form a BEC. In Fig. 2b we show the mixed-estimators in both momentum (left column) and real (right column) space. At small t∥/J⟂≈0.3t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}\approx 0.3 (3), we see that ⟨P^s⟂​(𝐤)⟩\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{k})\rangle is fairly dispersive, while ⟨P^s⟂​(𝐫)⟩\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{r})\rangle decays quickly as a function of radial distance. This indicates that the pairs are de-localized in momentum space and tightly-bound in real space. By identifying rungs that are (un)occupied with a pair with an effective spin-1/21/2 up (down) particle, the system can be mapped to a XXZ model [4], with signatures for this correspondence visible already at the considered t∥/J⟂≈0.4t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}\approx 0.4 in our numerics (see SM [44]). In the opposite limit, when the intralayer hopping t∥t_{\parallel} dominates over J⟂J_{\perp}, the interlayer pairs become spatially extended and behave as BCS Cooper pairs [4]. This is visible as a peak in ⟨P^s⟂​(𝐤)⟩\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{k})\rangle at the Fermi surface and a spatially extended, oscillating, real space pairing amplitude estimated by ⟨P^s⟂​(𝐫)⟩\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{r})\rangle in Fig. 2b (1) for t∥/J⟂≈1.7t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}\approx 1.7. The average particle distance lδl_{\delta} is indicated by the gray circles.

In the following, we will extend our analysis to different dopings δ=0.25,0.5,0.75\delta=0.25,0.5,0.75. For a more detailed analysis of the BEC-to-BCS crossover, we consider the real-space pairing and define the BEC and BCS regimes by the weight of |⟨P^s⟂​(𝐫)⟩||\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{r})\rangle| for 𝐫\mathbf{r} within and outside lδl_{\delta}. For the dopings considered, lδl_{\delta} ranges from lδ=0.25≈1.15l_{\delta=0.25}\approx 1.15 to lδ=0.75=2l_{\delta=0.75}=2. More precisely, we define the BEC (BCS) regime by ⟨Wδ⟩:=∑|𝐫|<lδ|⟨P^s⟂​(𝐫)⟩|/∑|𝐫|≥lδ|⟨P^s⟂​(𝐫)⟩|≥1\langle W_{\delta}\rangle:=\sum_{|\mathbf{r}|<l_{\delta}}|\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{r})\rangle|/\sum_{|\mathbf{r}|\geq l_{\delta}}|\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{r})\rangle|\geq 1 (⟨Wδ⟩<1\langle W_{\delta}\rangle<1). As shown in Fig. 2c, this condition reveals a BEC-to-BCS transition at t∥/J⟂≈0.5​(0.8)t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}\approx 0.5(0.8) for δ=0.75​(0.5)\delta=0.75(0.5), and no transition in the considered regimes of t∥/J⟂t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp} for δ=0.25\delta=0.25, in agreement with the phase diagram in Fig. 2a.

Our findings demonstrate the presence of a BEC-to-BCS crossover beyond the indications for such a crossover in coupled ladders found in Ref. [41], and offers insights into the microscopic origin of superconductivity in these materials: The presence of a BEC-to-BCS crossover is closely tied to a recently proposed pairing mechanism based on a Feshbach resonance between BEC and BCS-like pairing channels for both cuprate and bilayer nickelate superconductors [18, 19, 20, 5, 41, 45].

Pairing Symmetries.— In Fig. 3a we show the long-range contributions to the pair-pair correlation function

⟨⟨(Δ^centerΓ)†​Δ^edgeΓ⟩⟩=14​∑e∈ℰ⟨⟨(Δ^(Lx/2,Ly/2)Γ)†​Δ^eΓ⟩⟩\displaystyle\langle\!\langle(\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{center}})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{edge}}\rangle\rangle=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\mathrm{e}\in\mathcal{E}}\langle\!\langle(\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{(L_{x}/2,L_{y}/2)})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{e}}\rangle\rangle (7)

with (Δ^𝐢Γ)(†)(\hat{\Delta}^{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{i}})^{(\dagger)} restricted to pairs with size |𝐫|=1|\mathbf{r}|=1, and the system edges denoted by ℰ={(0,0),(0,Ly−1),(Lx−1,0),(Lx−1,Ly−1)}\mathcal{E}=\{(0,0),(0,L_{y}-1),(L_{x}-1,0),(L_{x}-1,L_{y}-1)\}. In agreement with Refs. [46, 12, 34], we observe a sudden change in the long-range pair-pair correlation symmetry when increasing J∥J_{\parallel} above J∥c≈t∥J^{c}_{\parallel}\approx t_{\parallel}, where ⟨⟨(Δ^centers⟂)†​Δ^edges⟂⟩⟩\langle\!\langle(\hat{\Delta}^{s_{\perp}}_{\mathrm{center}})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{s_{\perp}}_{\mathrm{edge}}\rangle\rangle drops to zero, while ⟨⟨(Δ^centerd∥)†​Δ^edged∥⟩⟩\langle\!\langle(\hat{\Delta}^{d_{\parallel}}_{\mathrm{center}})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{d_{\parallel}}_{\mathrm{edge}}\rangle\rangle increases from zero to a finite value. This sudden change is furthermore reflected in the respective mixed-estimators, ⟨⟨p^s⟂​(𝐤)⟩⟩\langle\langle\hat{p}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{k})\rangle\rangle and ⟨⟨p^d∥​(𝐤)⟩⟩\langle\langle\hat{p}^{d_{\parallel}}(\mathbf{k})\rangle\rangle, in Fig. 3b, for which we also observe a change in the signal amplitude from zero to a finite value when tuning J∥J_{\parallel} above or below J∥c≈t∥J^{c}_{\parallel}\approx t_{\parallel}. In contrast to the pair-pair correlations, the mixed-estimators also take into account contributions from more spatially extended pairs beyond nearest-neighbors, and are hence more general than the pair-pair correlations. All observations indicate a first-order phase transition at J∥cJ_{\parallel}^{c} [46, 12, 34]. To exclude the possibility of different pairing symmetries (like s∥s_{\parallel}), we provide a more detailed analysis in the SM [44].

Conclusions.— In this work, we have applied neural quantum states (NQS) – specifically a new combination of Gutzwiller projection with the recently developed Hidden Fermion Pfaffian States (HFPS) – to the mixed-dimensional bilayer tt-JJ model, motivated by the bilayer superconductor La3Ni2O7 (LNO) and recent cold atom simulations. We have achieved the first fully 2D study of this system that includes strong correlation effects. Our results establish that NQS can reliably capture both ground-state energies and subtle pairing phenomena in fermionic bilayers, including a BEC-to-BCS crossover and a first-order transition between interlayer ss-wave and intralayer dd-wave pairing symmetries. These observations enable insights into the microscopic origin of pairing in the mixD model and, more generally, superconductors like LNO. Beyond the specific application to the mixD bilayer system, this study highlights that NQS provide a powerful and flexible framework for studying strongly correlated fermionic systems and can access regimes beyond what has been explored with conventional methods. Looking ahead, the present work paves the way for the simulation of systems relevant to real materials and quantum simulation platforms using NQS.

Appendix A Connection of mixed-dimensional bilayers to LNO

LNO has a bilayer structure with two nickel-oxide layers connected by vertical Ni-O-Ni bonds. The onset of superconductivity under applied pressure of 1414 GPa is accompanied by a structural transition from the A​m​a​mAmam phase to the higher-symmetry F​m​m​mFmmm phase, where the vertical bond angle changes from 168∘168^{\circ} to 180∘180^{\circ} [43]. The increase in interlayer coupling during this transition suggests that stronger interlayer coupling enhances superconductivity.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations have revealed that the relevant orbitals near the Fermi level in LNO are given by the Ni 3​dx2−y23d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} and 3​dz23d_{z^{2}} orbitals, see Fig. 1a,

ℋ^2​o=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{2o}= −tx​y∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩,μ,σ𝒫^G((c^𝐢,μ,σ(x2−y2))†c^𝐣,μ,σ(x2−y2)+h.c.)𝒫^G−tz∑𝐢⟩,σ𝒫^G((c^𝐢,0,σ(z2))†c^𝐣,1,σ(z2)+h.c.)𝒫^G\displaystyle-t_{xy}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i,j}\rangle,\mu,\sigma}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{G}\left((\hat{c}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu,\sigma})^{\dagger}\hat{c}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},\mu,\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{G}-t_{z}\sum_{\mathbf{i}\rangle,\sigma}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{G}\left((\hat{c}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},0,\sigma})^{\dagger}\hat{c}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},1,\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{G}
+Jx​y∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩,μ𝐒^(x2−y2)𝐢,μ⋅𝐒^(x2−y2)𝐣,μ+Jz∑𝐢𝐒^(z2)𝐢,0⋅𝐒^(z2)𝐣,1−JH∑𝐢,α𝐒^(z2)𝐢,μ⋅𝐒^(x2−y2)𝐣,μ,\displaystyle+J_{xy}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i,j}\rangle,\mu}\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},\mu}+J_{z}\sum_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},0}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},1}-J_{H}\sum_{\mathbf{i},\alpha}\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},\mu}, (S1)

with the annihilation (creation) operators for the two orbitals, (c^𝐢,μ,σ(x2−y2))(†)(\hat{c}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu,\sigma})^{(\dagger)} and (c^𝐢,μ,σ(z2))(†)(\hat{c}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu,\sigma})^{(\dagger)}, and spin operators 𝐒^𝐢,μ(x2−y2)\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu} and 𝐒^𝐢,μ(z2)\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},\mu}. Inter-(intra-) layer hopping of the dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} (dz2d_{z^{2}}) orbitals vanishes due to their orbital character displayed in Fig. 1a. The dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} orbitals are approximately quarter-filled; the dz2d_{z^{2}} orbitals half-filled [43, 29, 49, 40]. Hence, the contribution of the tzt_{z} term vanishes. The 3​d3d character of the electronic structure together with the absence of perfect nesting in the non- interacting model as well as the minor role of electron-phonon coupling suggested by experiments [24] and theory [47] indicates that strong electronic correlations must be taken into account for an accurate description of LNO [25, 13, 6].

The strong interlayer interactions dominated by the almost localized dz2d_{z^{2}} have been shown to be promoted to the 3​dx2−y23d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} orbitals through a Hund’s coupling which favors a spin-triplet between the two orbitals [6, 27]. Integrating out the dz2d_{z^{2}} degrees of freedom yields a mixed-dimensional (mixD) bilayer t∥t_{\parallel}-J∥J_{\parallel}-J⟂J_{\perp} model shown in Fig. 1a (right) and given by Eq. (1) [35, 34, 27]. This can be seen as follows:

In the limit of strong JHJ_{H}, triplets form between the orbitals, and the low-energy subspace consists of the triplet states

|+1⟩𝐢,μ\displaystyle\ket{+1}_{\mathbf{i},\mu} =|↑⏟dz2​orbital​↑⏟dx2−y2​orbital⟩𝐢,μ\displaystyle=|\underbrace{\uparrow}_{d_{z^{2}}\,\mathrm{orbital}}\underbrace{\uparrow}_{d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}\,\mathrm{orbital}}\rangle_{\mathbf{i},\mu} (S2)
|0⟩𝐢,μ\displaystyle\ket{0}_{\mathbf{i},\mu} =12(|↑↓⟩𝐢,μ+|↓↑⟩𝐢,μ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle_{\mathbf{i},\mu}+|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle_{\mathbf{i},\mu}\right)
|−1⟩𝐢,μ\displaystyle\ket{-1}_{\mathbf{i},\mu} =|↓↓⟩𝐢,μ.\displaystyle=|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle_{\mathbf{i},\mu}.

For each rung, this results in nine low-energy states. It can be shown that the action of the operator ℋ^z2=𝐒^𝐢,0(z2)⋅𝐒^𝐣,1(z2)\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{z^{2}}=\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},0}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(z^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},1} corresponds to the action of ℋ^x2−y2=𝐒^𝐢,0(x2−y2)⋅𝐒^𝐣,1(x2−y2)\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{x^{2}-y^{2}}=\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{i},0}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{(x^{2}-y^{2})}_{\mathbf{j},1} for these states [27]. This allows to integrate out the dz2d_{z^{2}} orbitals by replacing the ℋ^z2\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{z^{2}} term in Eq. (S1) with ℋ^x2−y2\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{x^{2}-y^{2}}.

Appendix B Wave function amplitudes of Hidden Fermion Pfaffian States

In their unprojected form, the HFPS are defined as

|ψ⟩=1(Ntot/2)!​(∑p<q𝐅p​qv​v​c^p†​c^q†+∑p~<q~𝐅p~​q~h​h​d^p~†​d^q~†+∑p,p~𝐅p​p~v​h​c^p†​d^p~†)Ntot/2​|0⟩,\displaystyle|\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{(N_{\mathrm{tot}}/2)!}\Big(\sum_{p<q}\mathbf{F}^{vv}_{pq}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{p}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{q}+\sum_{\tilde{p}<\tilde{q}}\mathbf{F}^{hh}_{\tilde{p}\tilde{q}}\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{\tilde{p}}\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{\tilde{q}}+\sum_{p,\tilde{p}}\mathbf{F}^{vh}_{p\tilde{p}}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{p}\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{\tilde{p}}\Big)^{{N_{\mathrm{tot}}}/{2}}|0\rangle, (S3)

where c^p†\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{p} and d^p~†\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{\tilde{p}} denote visible and hidden fermion creation operators; and 𝐅v​v\mathbf{F}^{vv}, 𝐅h​h\mathbf{F}^{hh}, and 𝐅v​h\mathbf{F}^{vh} are matrices representing the respective couplings between visible and hidden fermions. The projection of Eq. (S3) onto Fock state configurations |𝐧⟩=|n1,n2,…,nN⟩\ket{\mathbf{n}}=\ket{n_{1},n_{2},\dots,n_{N}}, |ψ⟩\ket{\psi} is done by making the hidden configurations dependent on the physical 𝐧\mathbf{n}, i.e. 𝐧~=𝐧~​(𝐧)\tilde{\mathbf{n}}=\tilde{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{n}). This is done by defining the operation ⋆\star representing a slicing operation selecting the rows of 𝐅\mathbf{F} by 𝐧⋆𝐅\mathbf{n}\star\mathbf{F} and columns by 𝐅⋆𝐧\mathbf{F}\star\mathbf{n} according to the occupied orbitals of 𝐧\mathbf{n} and defining new hidden matrices 𝐅v​h​(𝐧):=𝐅v​h⋆𝐧~​(𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{vh}(\mathbf{{n}}):=\mathbf{F}^{vh}\star\mathbf{{\tilde{n}}}(\mathbf{{n}}) and 𝐅h​h​(𝐧):=𝐧~​(𝐧)⋆𝐅v​h⋆𝐧~​(𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{hh}(\mathbf{{n}}):=\mathbf{{\tilde{n}}}(\mathbf{{n}})\star\mathbf{F}^{vh}\star\mathbf{{\tilde{n}}}(\mathbf{{n}}), we have

ψ⁡(𝐧)=⟨𝐧|ψ⟩=pf⁡(𝐧⋆𝐅v​v⋆𝐧𝐧⋆𝐅θv​h​(𝐧)−𝐅v​hθ(𝐧)T⋆𝐧𝐅θh​h​(𝐧)).\psi(\mathbf{n})=\langle\mathbf{n}|\psi\rangle=\mathrm{pf}\!\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{n}\star\mathbf{F}^{vv}\star\mathbf{n}&\mathbf{n}\star\mathbf{F}^{vh}_{\mathbf{\theta}}(\mathbf{n})\\ -\mathbf{F}^{vh}_{\mathbf{\theta}}(\mathbf{n})^{T}\star\mathbf{n}&\mathbf{F}^{hh}_{\mathbf{\theta}}(\mathbf{n})\end{array}\right). (S4)

Hereby, pf\mathrm{pf} represents the calculation of the Pfaffian. The hidden contributions can be rewritten are parameterized by a neural network [10] with parameters θ\mathbf{\theta}. In this work, we use the slightly modified version, Eq. (2), where the configuration dependence of 𝐅θh​h​(𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{hh}_{\mathbf{\theta}}(\mathbf{n}) is absorbed into a Jastrow factor Jθ​(𝐧)J_{\mathbf{\theta}}(\mathbf{n}).

Appendix C Symmetries in Hidden Fermion Pfaffian States

For all calculations, we make use of the lattice symmetries of the bilayer setup. Here, we explain how the symmetrization is done, how the symmetry sectors are chosen and how the symmetrization is made computationally efficient. We closely follow Ref. [10] in this section.

For a fermionic Hamiltonian and spinless fermions, we consider the group of symmetry operations GG, with elements g∈Gg\in G and gg representing translations, rotations, reflections etc. of the system. The respective symmetry operators g^\hat{g} act on the Fock state basis as

g^​|𝐧⟩=∏iNc^g​𝐱i†​|0⟩=Π⁡(𝐧,g)​|g​𝐧⟩,\hat{g}|\mathbf{n}\rangle=\prod_{i}^{N}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{g\mathbf{x}_{i}}|0\rangle=\Pi(\mathbf{n},g)\,|g\mathbf{n}\rangle, (S5)

with g​𝐧g\mathbf{n} the new occupation numbers after application of gg, and Πg​(𝐧)=±1\Pi_{g}(\mathbf{n})=\pm 1 is the additional sign associated with fermion permutations accompanying gg.

The symmetrized wave function is given by

ψsym​(𝐧)\displaystyle\psi_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbf{n}) =∑gΠg​(𝐧)​χg​ψ​(g​𝐧)\displaystyle=\sum_{g}\Pi_{g}(\mathbf{n})\,\chi_{g}\,\psi(g\mathbf{n}) (S6)

with the character of the symmetry operation χg\chi_{g}. For the HFPS (2), ψ⁡(g​𝐧)\psi(g\mathbf{n}) is given by

ψ⁡(g​𝐧)=pf⁡((g​𝐧)⋆𝐅v​v⋆(g​𝐧)(g​𝐧)⋆𝐅v​h​(g​𝐧)−𝐅v​h(g𝐧)T⋆(g𝐧)𝐅h​h​(g​𝐧)).\psi(g\mathbf{n})=\mathrm{pf}\!\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}(g\mathbf{n})\star\mathbf{F}^{vv}\star(g\mathbf{n})&(g\mathbf{n})\star\mathbf{F}^{vh}(g\mathbf{n})\\ -\mathbf{F}^{vh}(g\mathbf{n})^{T}\star(g\mathbf{n})&\mathbf{F}^{hh}(g\mathbf{n})\end{array}\right). (S7)

As explained in the following, we use Group Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) to calculate 𝐅v​h​(𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{vh}(\mathbf{n}) and 𝐅v​h​(𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{vh}(\mathbf{n}), which have the advantage that 𝐅v​h​(g​𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{vh}(g\mathbf{n}) and 𝐅v​h​(g​𝐧)\mathbf{F}^{vh}(g\mathbf{n}) can be obtained from a single forward pass. The Pfaffian however has to be computed for every gg in Eq. (S7) separately. In Sec. C.3, we explain how the cost can be reduced by applying translational symmetries only on the level of a sublattice unit cell.

C.1 Group Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs)

Group Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a generalization of CNNs that work for non-abelian symmetry groups. These are useful for lattices, which have symmetry groups with rotations, reflections, and translations, some of which do not commute. These are constructed using equivariant convolutions, i.e. linear operations that preserve the structure of a discrete symmetry group [39]. This is in contrast to symmetry-averaging procedures which have been applied in various works [22].

In this paper, we consider the symmetry group of the square lattice GG, including translations and the D4D_{4} symmetry group. A set of objects SS is called the GG-space if the objects are related by symmetry transformations of GG. Each group convolutional layer defines a linear transformation between these GG-spaces. Given a set of feature vectors, {𝐟}S={𝐟⁡(s)|s∈S}\{\mathbf{f}\}_{S}=\{\mathbf{f}(s)|s\in S\}, a function is equivariant if it obeys the constraint

F⁡(g​{𝐟}S)=g​F​({𝐟}S),\displaystyle F(g\{\mathbf{f}\}_{S})=gF(\{\mathbf{f}\}_{S}), (S8)

where g∈Gg\in G are the elements of the symmetry group. In short, the layer transformations must commute with the symmetry generators of the group 11 1 The actual equivariant constraint is looser, as the operation only has to preserve the structure of the group, as the set can be arbitrarily permuted. For ease of explanation we consider the case where the ordering of the set stays the same.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) consist of convolutional layers with feature maps 𝐟\mathbf{f} and kernels 𝐤\mathbf{k}. While the kernel 𝐤\mathbf{k} is slid over the input features, resulting in different translations (x−x′,y−y′)(x-x^{\prime},y-y^{\prime}) it is multiplied with the input feature values 𝐟⁡(x′,y′)\mathbf{f}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}), resulting in

C⁡(x,y)=[𝐟∗𝐤]​(x,y)=∑x′,y′∑iki​(x−x′,y−y′)​fi​(x′,y′).\displaystyle C(x,y)=[\mathbf{f}*\mathbf{k}](x,y)=\sum_{x^{\prime},y^{\prime}}\sum_{i}k_{i}(x-x^{\prime},y-y^{\prime})\,f_{i}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}). (S9)

The index ii denotes the ii-th channel of the input feature. The GCNN generalizes the CNN to act over a more general discrete group GG,

C⁡(g)=∑h∈G∑iki​(g−1​h)​fi​(h).\displaystyle C(g)=\sum_{h\in G}\sum_{i}k_{i}(g^{-1}h)\,f_{i}(h). (S10)

This general group convolution is equivariant under a group operation uu since [39]

C⁡(u​g)=∑h∈G∑iki​(g−1​u−1​h)​fi​(h)=∑h′∈G∑iki​(g−1​h′)​fi​(u​h′)=u​C​(g).\displaystyle C(ug)=\sum_{h\in G}\sum_{i}k_{i}(g^{-1}u^{-1}h)\,f_{i}(h)=\sum_{h^{\prime}\in G}\sum_{i}k_{i}(g^{-1}h^{\prime})\,f_{i}(uh^{\prime})=uC(g). (S11)

C.2 Choice of Symmetry Sectors

Since we make use of the translational, rotational and spin-flip symmetry of the system, we perform scans through these symmetry sectors in order to obtain the symmetry sector of the ground state. Exemplary scans of the translational symmetry sector for 4×4×24\times 4\times 2 mixD bilayers at different dopings δ=0.62,0.5,0.25\delta=0.62,0.5,0.25 are shown in Fig. S1.

C.3 Sublattice symmetries

In general, Eq. S7 requires applying summing over |G||G| Pfaffians. However, the number of unique Pfaffians in the sum can be reduced by imposing symmetries on the couplings between visible fermions, Fv​vF^{vv}. For example if the couplings between electrons are translationally invariant, only point group symmetries need to be restored. In practice, we find that it is best to choose the couplings of Fv​vF_{vv} to have ”sublattice symmetry”. Here a unit cell with several different sub-lattices is defined, and translational symmetry is enforced for the sublattices but not within the unit cell. This is explained in detail in Ref. [10].

In practice, we determine the sublattice size Wx×Wy×WzW_{x}\times W_{y}\times W_{z} by a scan, choosing the sublattice geometry that produces the lowest ground state energy. Exemplary scans for 8×8×28\times 8\times 2 systems at different dopings δ=0.5,0.25\delta=0.5,0.25 and J∥/J⟂=0.4,3.0J_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}=0.4,3.0 respectively – corresponding to states with ss- and dd- wave pairing –, are shown in Fig. S2.

Appendix D Convergence of the G-HFPS

D.1 Optimization

D.1.1 Stochastic reconfiguration

We optimize the G-HFPS using the minimum-step stochastic reconfiguration algorithm from Refs. [7, 36], with a pseudo-inverse with relative singular value cutoff δ=10−12\delta=10^{-12}, learning rate η=0.01\eta=0.01 and 1000010000 samples in each iteration.

For the transfer learning, we use a similar algorithm that explicitly follows the respective state under consideration as a function of the Hamiltonian parameters λ\mathbf{\lambda} fro Ref. [31], which is summarized in the following section.

D.1.2 Adiabatic transport

For the scans of the phase diagram in the main text, Figs. 2 and 3, we use the adiabatic transport protocol developed in Ref. [31], which is specifically taylored to follow an eigenstate when evolving the Hamiltonian parameters.

For a given target eigenenergy of an Hamiltonian ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}, ωλ\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}}, we estimate the target eigenstate |Ψλ⟩|\Psi_{\mathbf{\lambda}}\rangle by the sequence (starting from a state |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle)

|Ψ⟩=limk→∞|Ψk⟩=limk→∞[(ℋλ−ωλ)−1]k​|Ψ0⟩=limk→∞(ℋλ−ωλ)−k​|Ψ0⟩=limk→∞∑ncn​(Eλ​(σn)−ωλ)−k​|σn⟩,|\Psi\rangle=\lim_{k\to\infty}|\Psi_{k}\rangle=\lim_{k\to\infty}\left[(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}})^{-1}\right]^{k}|\Psi_{0}\rangle=\lim_{k\to\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}})^{-k}|\Psi_{0}\rangle=\lim_{k\to\infty}\sum_{n}c_{n}(E_{\mathbf{\lambda}}(\mathbf{\sigma}_{n})-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}})^{-k}|\mathbf{\sigma}_{n}\rangle, (S12)

converging to the ground state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle after a sufficient number of iterations kk.

For a variational state parameterized by network parameters θ\mathbf{\theta}, the new state after an infinitesimal change in parameters can be expanded as

|Ψθ+δ​θ⟩≈|Ψθ⟩+∑μδ​θμ​|∂μΨθ⟩,|\Psi_{\theta+\delta\theta}\rangle\approx|\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle+\sum_{\mu}\delta\theta_{\mu}|\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle, (S13)

where |∂μΨθ⟩=∂∂θμ​|Ψθ⟩|\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{\mu}}|\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle. Projecting one step of Eq. (S12) onto the tangent space of the variational manifold, multiplying from the left by (ℋλ−ωλ)(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}}) and taking inner products with the tangent vectors ⟨∂μΨθ|\langle\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}|, yields

∑νRe⁡[⟨∂μΨθ|(ℋλ−ωλ)|∂νΨθ⟩]​δ​θν=−Re⁡[⟨∂μΨθ|ℋλ|Ψθ⟩].\sum_{\nu}\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\langle\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}|(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}})|\partial_{\nu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle\right]\delta\theta_{\nu}=-\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\langle\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}|\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}|\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle\right]. (S14)

Equation (S14) defines a linear system for the parameter updates, which we write compactly as [31]

𝐆​δ​θ=−𝐟,\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{\delta\theta}=-\mathbf{f}, (S15)

where the generalized covariance matrix 𝐆\mathbf{G} and force vector 𝐟\mathbf{f} are

Gμ​ν\displaystyle G_{\mu\nu} =2​Re​[⟨∂μΨθ|(ℋλ−ωλ)|∂νΨθ⟩],\displaystyle=2\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\langle\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}|(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}})|\partial_{\nu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle\right], (S16)
fμ\displaystyle f_{\mu} =2​Re​[⟨∂μΨθ|ℋλ|Ψθ⟩].\displaystyle=2\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\langle\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}|\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}|\Psi_{\mathbf{\theta}}\rangle\right]. (S17)

The update is implemented by defining the local energy Eloc,λ​(σ)=⟨σ|H|Ψθ⟩⟨σ|Ψθ⟩E_{\mathrm{loc},\mathbf{\lambda}}(\mathbf{\sigma})=\frac{\langle\mathbf{\sigma}|H|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{\sigma}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}, the Jacobian

Jμ​(σ)\displaystyle J_{\mu}(\mathbf{\sigma}) =⟨σ|∂μΨθ⟩⟨σ|Ψθ⟩,\displaystyle=\frac{\langle\mathbf{\sigma}|\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{\sigma}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}, (S18)

and the projected Jacobian

Pμ​(σ)\displaystyle P_{\mu}(\mathbf{\sigma}) =⟨σ|(ℋλ−ωλ)|∂μΨθ⟩⟨σ|Ψθ⟩=∂μEloc,λ​(σ)+Jμ​(σ)​(Eloc,λ​(σ)−ωλ)\displaystyle=\frac{\langle\mathbf{\sigma}|(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{\lambda}}-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}})|\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{\sigma}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}=\partial_{\mu}E_{\mathrm{loc},\mathbf{\lambda}}(\mathbf{\sigma})+J_{\mu}(\mathbf{\sigma})\bigl(E_{\mathrm{loc},\mathbf{\lambda}}(\mathbf{\sigma})-\omega_{\mathbf{\lambda}}\bigr) (S19)

Replacing Ji​μ=Jμ​(σi)/NsJ_{i\mu}=J_{\mu}(\mathbf{\sigma}_{i})/\sqrt{N_{s}}, Pi​μ=Pμ​(σi)/NsP_{i\mu}=P_{\mu}(\mathbf{\sigma}_{i})/\sqrt{N_{s}}, and εi=Eloc​(σi)/Ns\varepsilon_{i}=E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{\sigma}_{i})/\sqrt{N_{s}}, the update equation reduces to the linear system

J⊤​P​δ​θ=−J⊤​ε,J^{\top}P\,\delta\theta=-\,J^{\top}\varepsilon, (S20)

which is solved similarly to the stochastic reconfiguration update [31].

D.2 Mean-Field initialization

We start the optimization of the G-HFPS from a (Gutzwiller projected) mean-field solution of

H\displaystyle H =−tMF∑⟨i,j⟩,σ(ci​σ†cj​σ+h.c.)+UMF∑ini↑ni↓+∑i,j(Δi​jMFci↑†cj↓†+h.c.).\displaystyle=-t^{\mathrm{MF}}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle,\sigma}\left(c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)+U^{\mathrm{MF}}\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}+\sum_{i,j}\bigl(\Delta_{ij}^{\mathrm{MF}}\,c^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{j\downarrow}+\text{h.c.}\bigr). (S21)

We consider the following pairing fields

Δ^s⟂MF\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}^{\mathrm{MF}}_{s_{\perp}} ∝(c^𝐥,0,↓​c^𝐥,1,↑−c^𝐥,0,↑​c^𝐥,1,↓)\displaystyle\propto\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},0,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},1,\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},0,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},1,\downarrow}\right) (S22)
Δ^d∥,μMF\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}_{d_{\parallel},\mu}^{\mathrm{MF}} ∝∑δ=±x^,±y^ηδd​(c^𝐥,μ,↓​c^𝐥+δ,μ,↑−c^𝐥,μ,↑​c^𝐥+δ,μ,↓)\displaystyle\propto\sum_{\delta=\pm\hat{x},\pm\hat{y}}{\eta_{\delta}^{d}}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},\mu,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l}+\delta,\mu,\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},\mu,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l}+\delta,\mu,\downarrow}\right)
Δ^s∥,μMF\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}_{s_{\parallel},\mu}^{\mathrm{MF}} ∝∑δ=±x^,±y^(c^𝐥,μ,↓​c^𝐥+δ,μ,↑−c^𝐥,μ,↑​c^𝐥+δ,μ,↓)\displaystyle\propto\sum_{\delta=\pm\hat{x},\pm\hat{y}}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},\mu,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l}+\delta,\mu,\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},\mu,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l}+\delta,\mu,\downarrow}\right)
Δ^s⟂+d∥MF\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}_{s_{\perp}+d_{\parallel}}^{\mathrm{MF}} ∝Δ^s⟂+Δ^d∥,0+Δ^d∥,1.\displaystyle\propto\hat{\Delta}_{s_{\perp}}+\hat{\Delta}_{d_{\parallel},0}+\hat{\Delta}_{d_{\parallel},1}.

The mean-field solution is obtained by using exact gradient descent. In practice, we use UMF/tMF=3.0U^{\mathrm{MF}}/t^{\mathrm{MF}}=3.0 and use constant pairing fields Δ⟂MF\Delta_{\perp}^{\mathrm{MF}} (Δ∥MF\Delta_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{MF}}) between (within) the layers or both. Δ⟂MF\Delta_{{}_{\perp}}^{\mathrm{MF}} and Δ∥MF\Delta_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{MF}} are chosen according to the lowest energy obtained after the optimization of the full G-HFPS, initializing with the respective MF solution. Exemplary results for a 8×8×28\times 8\times 2 bilayer at quarter-filling and different pairing fields Δ⟂MF/tMF\Delta_{\perp}^{\mathrm{MF}}/t^{\mathrm{MF}} and Δ∥MF/tMF\Delta_{\parallel}^{\mathrm{MF}}/t^{\mathrm{MF}} are shown in Fig. S3 for two different regions in the phase diagram with interlayer ss-wave and intralayer dd-wave pairing, respectively. We always apply the respective Δ⟂(∥)MF\Delta_{\perp(\parallel)}^{\mathrm{MF}}, while setting the other Δ∥(⟂)MF=0\Delta_{\parallel(\perp)}^{\mathrm{MF}}=0. It can be seen that in both cases the energy obtained with a small pairing field Δ⟂,∥MF/tMF=0.1\Delta_{\perp,\parallel}^{\mathrm{MF}}/t^{\mathrm{MF}}=0.1 yields a significantly higher energy than Δ⟂,∥MF/tMF≥1.0\Delta_{\perp,\parallel}^{\mathrm{MF}}/t^{\mathrm{MF}}\geq 1.0. The pairing correlations right after the MF optimization are shown in Fig. S4.

D.3 Number of parameters

Throughout most of the work, we consider Nh=4N_{h}=4 hidden fermions and a GCNN feature dimension of f=10f=10. Fig. S5 shows that increasing the number of parameters further does not improve the energy significantly for the considered 500 training steps.

D.4 Spatial Symmetries

In Fig. S6, we show the optimization curves with all symmetries imposed (blue) and without the C4C_{4} rotational symmetry (green). The final energy increases by approx. 0.1%0.1\% relative to the full symmetrization when the rotational symmetry is not taken into account (decreasing the computational cost by a factor of 44).

D.5 Number of optimization steps

If not stated differently, the G-HFPS considered in this work are trained for 1500 optimization steps. In the last 500 steps, the energy does not improve significantly. Furthermore, other observables like the real-space mixed-estimator do not change significantly after 500 optimization steps, see Fig. S7.

D.6 Convergence for different regions of the phase diagram

The convergence differs for different regions in the phase diagram, as we show exemplarily in Fig. S8 for 4×4×24\times 4\times 2 mixD bilayers with doping δ=0.5\delta=0.5: Comparing different parameters J⟂/t∥=0.6,J∥/t∥=0.4J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=0.6,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.4, J⟂/t∥=3.0,J∥/t∥=0.0J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=3.0,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.0 and J⟂/t∥=10.0,J∥/t∥=0.0J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=10.0,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.0, we find that convergence is enhanced for J⟂≫J∥J_{\perp}\gg J_{\parallel}. This corresponds to the regime where the system can be mapped to a XXZ model (Heisenberg model for δ=0.5\delta=0.5).

D.7 System Size

In addition to the energies for different system sizes shown in Fig. 1 in the main text (and reprinted in Fig. S9 (left)), further quantities can be compared as a function of the system sizes. Here, we additionally show the interlayer ss-wave pairing correlations (see Fig. S9 (left and right) for two points in the mixD parameter space. All quantities are relatively constant as w.r.t. the system size. In Sec. F, also the system size scaling of the mixed estimator will be considered.

D.8 Comparison to MPS

In addition to the comparison of energies from the G-HFPS (NQS) and MPS in 1b, we also compare the bond-spin correlations 1/2∑iy⟨S^(ix,iy,0)⋅S^(ix,iy,1)⟩1/2\sum_{i_{y}}\langle\hat{S}_{(i_{x},i_{y},0)}\cdot\hat{S}_{(i_{x},i_{y},1)}\rangle and densities ∑iy,iz⟨n^(ix,iy,iz)⟩\sum_{i_{y},i_{z}}\langle\hat{n}_{(i_{x},i_{y},i_{z})}\rangle in Fig. S10 for the 32×2×232\times 2\times 2 system. As in Fig. 1, we consider quarter-filling and different parameters J⟂/t∥,J∥/t∥J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel},\,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}. In all considered cases, we find very good agreement between the different methods, with the largest discrepancies at the boundaries due to the different boundary conditions that are applied in xx-direction (open boundaries for MPS; periodic boundaries for NQS).

D.8.1 Convergence of MPS

In Fig. S11, we show the energy and truncation error of the MPS with increasing bond dimension. The final truncation error for J⟂/t∥=3.0J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=3.0 and J∥/t∥=0.0J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.0 (blue) is on the order of 10−810^{-8}, for J⟂/t∥=0.6J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=0.6 and J∥/t∥=0.4J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.4 (orange) on the order of 10−610^{-6}.

Appendix E Density-density correlations

In Fig. S12, we present density-density correlations within the layers (⟨n^μ​𝐢​n^μ​𝐣⟩\langle\hat{n}_{\mu\mathbf{i}}\hat{n}_{\mu\mathbf{j}}\rangle, top row) and between the layers (⟨n^0​𝐢​n^1​𝐣⟩\langle\hat{n}_{0\mathbf{i}}\hat{n}_{1\mathbf{j}}\rangle, bottom row). We consider two exemplary points in the phase diagram, J⟂/t∥=3.0,J∥/t∥=0.0J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=3.0,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.0 and J⟂/t∥=0.6,J∥/t∥=0.4J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=0.6,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.4, both at δ=0.5\delta=0.5, after 500500 optimization steps and exploiting the the full C4C_{4} symmetry of the system. The diagonal cuts reveal a stronger signal for interlayer density correlations when J⟂J_{\perp} is increased. The full density correlation maps for the corresponding J⟂/t∥=3.0,J∥/t∥=0.0J_{\perp}/t_{\parallel}=3.0,J_{\parallel}/t_{\parallel}=0.0 in the middle panel reveal relatively long-range signals in both inter- and intralayer density correlations, with a minimal value for nearest-neighbors. Decreasing J⟂J_{\perp} (right panel) this long-range signal vanishes, especially for the interlayer correlations.

Appendix F Mixed momentum-real space estimator

F.1 Approximating the pairing order parameter

In the main text, we consider the following pairing symmetries

Δ^𝐥s⟂\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}^{s_{\perp}}_{\mathbf{l}} ∝(c^𝐥,0,↓​c^𝐥,1,↑−c^𝐥,0,↑​c^𝐥,1,↓)\displaystyle\propto\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},0,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},1,\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},0,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},1,\downarrow}\right) (S23)
Δ^μ,𝐥d∥\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}^{d_{\parallel}}_{\mu,\mathbf{l}} ∝∑δ=±x^,±y^ηδd​(c^𝐥,μ,↓​c^𝐥+δ,μ,↑−c^𝐥,μ,↑​c^𝐥+δ,μ,↓).\displaystyle\propto\sum_{\delta=\pm\hat{x},\pm\hat{y}}{\eta_{\delta}^{d}}\left(\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},\mu,\downarrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l}+\delta,\mu,\uparrow}-\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l},\mu,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{l}+\delta,\mu,\downarrow}\right).

In order to study the pairing properties of the system, we would like to calculate the order parameter

Δ𝐤s⟂=⟨c^𝐤,0,↑​c^−𝐤,1,↓⟩andΔ𝐤,μd∥=⟨c^𝐤,μ,↑​c^−𝐤,μ,↓⟩\displaystyle\Delta^{s_{\perp}}_{\mathbf{k}}=\langle\hat{c}_{\mathbf{k},0,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{-k},1,\downarrow}\rangle\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\Delta^{d_{\parallel}}_{\mathbf{k},\mu}=\langle\hat{c}_{\mathbf{k},\mu,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{-k},\mu,\downarrow}\rangle (S24)

or the full pair-pair map

M𝐤,𝐤′s⟂=⟨c^−𝐤,1,↓†​c^𝐤,0,↑†​c^𝐤′,0,↑​c^−𝐤′,1,↓⟩andM𝐤,𝐤′,μd∥=⟨c^−𝐤,μ,↓†​c^𝐤,μ,↑†​c^𝐤′,μ,↑​c^−𝐤′,μ,↓⟩.\displaystyle M_{\mathbf{k,k^{\prime}}}^{s_{\perp}}=\langle\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{-k},1,\downarrow}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k},0,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{k^{\prime}},0,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{-k^{\prime}},1,\downarrow}\rangle\quad\mathrm{and}\quad M_{\mathbf{k,k^{\prime}},\mu}^{d_{\parallel}}=\langle\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{-k},\mu,\downarrow}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k},\mu,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{k^{\prime}},\mu,\uparrow}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{-k^{\prime}},\mu,\downarrow}\rangle. (S25)

In the following discussion, we absorb the layer index μ\mu into 𝐤\mathbf{k} for the intra-layer pairing. For finite-size systems and fixed particle number, we face the problem that Δ𝐤Γ=0\Delta^{\Gamma}_{\mathbf{k}}=0 even in the presence of superconductivity. For M𝐤,𝐤′M_{\mathbf{k,k^{\prime}}} the problem is that it involves (Lx​Ly)4(L_{x}L_{y})^{4} terms and is too expensive to evaluate. In order to still gain insights into these quantities, we consider the mixed-estimator defined in Eq. (5) in the main text and reprinted here for clarity:

⟨P^s⟂​(𝐤)⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{P}^{s_{\perp}}(\mathbf{k})\rangle =1⟨Δ¯†​Δ¯⟩1/2​⟨c^𝐤,1,↑†​c^−𝐤,0,↓†​Δ^𝐥s⟂⟩=1⟨Δ¯†​Δ¯⟩1/2​12​N​∑𝐢,𝐣ei​𝐤​(𝐢−𝐣)​⟨c^𝐢,1,↑†​c^𝐣,0,↓†​Δ^𝐥s⟂⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\bar{\Delta}^{\dagger}\bar{\Delta}\rangle^{1/2}}\langle\hat{c}_{\mathbf{k},1,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{-\mathbf{k},0,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{l}}^{s_{\perp}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\langle\bar{\Delta}^{\dagger}\bar{\Delta}\rangle^{1/2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}N}\sum_{\mathbf{i,j}}e^{i\mathbf{k}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})}\langle\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i},1,\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{j},0,\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}^{s_{\perp}}_{\mathbf{l}}\rangle. (S26)
⟨P^d∥​(𝐤)⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{P}^{d_{\parallel}}(\mathbf{k})\rangle =1⟨Δ¯†​Δ¯⟩1/2​⟨c^𝐤,↑†​c^−𝐤,↓†​Δ^𝐥d∥⟩=1⟨Δ¯†​Δ¯⟩1/2​1N​∑𝐢,𝐣ei​𝐤​(𝐢−𝐣)​⟨c^𝐢,↑†​c^𝐣,↓†​Δ^𝐥d∥⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\bar{\Delta}^{\dagger}\bar{\Delta}\rangle^{1/2}}\langle\hat{c}_{\mathbf{k},\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{-\mathbf{k},\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{l}}^{d_{\parallel}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\langle\bar{\Delta}^{\dagger}\bar{\Delta}\rangle^{1/2}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{i,j}}e^{i\mathbf{k}(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})}\langle\hat{c}_{\mathbf{i},\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{j},\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{l}}^{d_{\parallel}}\rangle. In the following, we consider the specific case of interlayer ss-wave pairing but the discussion can be straightforwardly adapted to the intralayer pairing. For simplicity, we absorb the layer indices 0,10,1 into the site indices 𝐢,𝐣\mathbf{i,j} and omit the symmetry label Γ\Gamma.

In what follows, we will motivate the use of (S26): In the presence of superconductivity, we expect that pair creation and annihilation processes become increasingly uncorrelated as the system size increases. This implies that MM is dominated by a single eigenvector

M𝐤,𝐤′=P𝐤​P𝐤′+𝒪⁡(1/N).\displaystyle M_{\mathbf{k,k^{\prime}}}=P_{\mathbf{k}}P_{\mathbf{k^{\prime}}}+\mathcal{O}(1/N). (S28)

and hence

F.2 Finite size scaling

In Fig. S13, the mixed estimator is shown for different system sizes N=4×4×2,4×8×2,8×8×2N=4\times 4\times 2,4\times 8\times 2,8\times 8\times 2 and δ=0.5\delta=0.5.

F.3 Estimating the size of the pairs: mixed-estimator in real space

Ekin=−⟨∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩,μ,σ𝒫^G​(c^𝐢,μ,σ†​c^𝐣,μ,σ+h.c.)⟩\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{kin}}=-\langle\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i,j}\rangle,\mu,\sigma}\mathcal{\hat{P}}_{G}\left(\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i},\mu,\sigma}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{j},\mu,\sigma}+\text{h.c.}\right)\rangle (S36)

and Epot=E−EkinE_{\mathrm{pot}}=E-E_{\mathrm{kin}}. The ratio Epot/Ekin≲0.5E_{\mathrm{pot}}/E_{\mathrm{kin}}\lesssim 0.5 throughout the considered regime of t∥/J⟂t_{\parallel}/J_{\perp}, i.e. the system is dominated by the kinetic energy. Appendix I The strong J⟂J_{\perp} limit of the mixed-dimensional model

I.1 The mapping

As shown in Ref. [4], the mixed-dimensional tt-JJ bilayer can be mapped to an effective spin-1/21/2 description when J⟂≫t∥,J∥J_{\perp}\gg t_{\parallel},J_{\parallel}. In this limit, the low-energy sector of the Hamiltonian (1) is restricted to two rung states at each lattice site 𝐢\mathbf{i}: The first corresponds to a pair of holes residing on the two layers, |0⟩𝐢=|0⟩𝐢,0​|0⟩𝐢,1\ket{0}_{\mathbf{i}}=\ket{0}_{\mathbf{i},0}\ket{0}_{\mathbf{i},1}, while the second is an interlayer spin singlet, |1⟩𝐢=b^𝐢†​|0⟩𝐢\ket{1}_{\mathbf{i}}=\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i}}\ket{0}_{\mathbf{i}} created by the operator

b^𝐢†​|0⟩𝐢=12​(c^𝐢,↑,0†​c^𝐢,↓,1†−c^𝐢,↓,0†​c^𝐢,↑,1†)​|0⟩i,\displaystyle\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i}}\ket{0}_{\mathbf{i}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i},\uparrow,0}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i},\downarrow,1}-\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i},\downarrow,0}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i},\uparrow,1}\right)\ket{0}_{\textbf{i}}, (S37)

and subject to the hard-core constraint b^𝐢†​b^𝐢≤1\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}\leq 1.

Carrying out a second-order perturbative expansion in the intralayer hopping, following Ref. [4] and related works [20, 19, 41], one finds that virtual hopping processes generate an effective hard-core boson model on a single square lattice. The emergent parameters are an effective boson hopping teff=2​t∥2/J⟂t_{\mathrm{eff}}=2t_{\parallel}^{2}/J_{\perp}, a nearest-neighbor density interaction Veff=4​t∥2/J⟂−J∥/2V_{\mathrm{eff}}=4t_{\parallel}^{2}/J_{\perp}-J_{\parallel}/2, and a chemical potential term μb=−J⟂−2​t∥2​z/J⟂\mu_{b}=-J_{\perp}-2t_{\parallel}^{2}z/J_{\perp}, where zz denotes the coordination number of the lattice (z=2z=2 for the bilayer geometry). Neglecting constant energy shifts, the effective Hamiltonian takes the form

ℋ^eff=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{eff}}= −teff∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩𝒫^(b^𝐢†b^𝐣+h.c.)𝒫^+μb∑𝐢b^𝐢†b^𝐢+Veff∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩b^𝐢†b^𝐢b^𝐣†b^𝐣.\displaystyle-t_{\mathrm{eff}}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\rangle}\hat{\mathcal{P}}\big(\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{j}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}+\text{h.c.}\big)\hat{\mathcal{P}}+\mu_{b}\sum_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}+V_{\mathrm{eff}}\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\rangle}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{j}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{j}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,. (S38)

An effective spin representation is obtained by identifying the two local bosonic configurations with the down and up states of a spin-1/21/2 system. Defining spin operators J^𝐢μ\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\mu} (μ=x,y,z\mu=x,y,z) via

J^𝐢+=(−1)𝐢b^†𝐢,J^𝐢−=(−1)𝐢b^𝐢,J^z𝐢=b^†𝐢b^𝐢−1/2,\begin{gathered}\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}^{+}=(-1)^{\mathbf{i}}\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i}},\quad\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}^{-}=(-1)^{\mathbf{i}}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}},\quad\hat{J}^{z}_{\mathbf{i}}=\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}-1/2,\end{gathered} (S39)

with (−1)𝐢=+1(-1)^{\mathbf{i}}=+1 (−1-1) on the A (B) sublattice, the hard-core boson Hamiltonian (S38) is mapped onto an XXZ spin model,

ℋ^XXZ=K​∑⟨𝐢,𝐣⟩(J^𝐢x​J^𝐣x+J^𝐢y​J^𝐣y+δ​J^𝐢z​J^𝐣z)+const.,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{XXZ}}=K\sum_{\langle\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\rangle}\left(\hat{J}^{x}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{J}^{x}_{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{J}^{y}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{J}^{y}_{\mathbf{j}}+\delta\hat{J}^{z}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{J}^{z}_{\mathbf{j}}\right)+\mathrm{const.}\,, (S40)

where K=4​t∥2/J⟂K=4t_{\parallel}^{2}/J_{\perp} and δ=1−J∥/(2​K)\delta=1-J_{\parallel}/(2K). The magnetization mm of the XXZ model (S40), is related to the particle density of the original bilayer by m=n−12m=n-\tfrac{1}{2}. For vanishing intralayer exchange J∥=0J_{\parallel}=0 and quarter filling, the model reduces to the 2D Heisenberg Hamiltonian.

I.2 Numerical signatures of the XXZ limit

We note that using Eq. (S39),

(Δ^𝐢s⟂)†​Δ^𝐣s⟂=b^𝐢†​b^𝐣=(−1)𝐢​(−1)𝐣​J^𝐢+​J^𝐣−.\displaystyle(\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{i}}^{s_{\perp}})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{j}}^{s_{\perp}}=\hat{b}_{\mathbf{i}}^{\dagger}\hat{b}_{\mathbf{j}}=(-1)^{\mathbf{i}}(-1)^{\mathbf{j}}\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}^{+}\hat{J}_{\mathbf{j}}^{-}. (S41)

For the Heiseinberg limit with m=0m=0 and emerging SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU(2)} symmetry (i.e. ⟨J^𝐢+​J^𝐣−⟩=2​⟨J^𝐢x​J^𝐣x⟩=2​⟨J^𝐢y​J^𝐣y⟩=2​⟨J^𝐢z​J^𝐣z⟩\langle\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}^{+}\hat{J}_{\mathbf{j}}^{-}\rangle=2\langle\hat{J}^{x}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{J}^{x}_{\mathbf{j}}\rangle=2\langle\hat{J}^{y}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{J}^{y}_{\mathbf{j}}\rangle=2\langle\hat{J}^{z}_{\mathbf{i}}\hat{J}^{z}_{\mathbf{j}}\rangle), this can be used to connect to the spin-spin correlator to the pair-pair correlations in the mixD bilayer,

J^𝐢⋅J^𝐣=32​(−1)𝐢​(−1)𝐣​(Δ^𝐢s⟂)†​Δ^𝐣s⟂.\displaystyle\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}\cdot\hat{J}_{\mathbf{j}}=\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{\mathbf{i}}(-1)^{\mathbf{j}}(\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{i}}^{s_{\perp}})^{\dagger}\hat{\Delta}_{\mathbf{j}}^{s_{\perp}}. (S42)

In Fig. S19, it can be seen that for strong J⟂J_{\perp} the system features effective spin correlations ⟨J^𝐢⋅J^𝐢+𝐫⟩\langle\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}}\cdot\hat{J}_{\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{r}}\rangle with long-range AFM order, as expected for the Heisenberg model.
